dx: Embolic left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke from atrial fibrillation
case: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after his wife noticed that he could not speak and could not lift his right arm. He has hypertension and intermittent palpitations for 1 year. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 112/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 164/92 mm Hg. Physical examination shows weakness of the right lower face, 1/5 strength in the right arm, and 4/5 strength in the right leg. His speech is sparse and effortful, and he cannot repeat a short phrase, but he follows two-step commands. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. A noncontrast CT scan of the head shows no hemorrhage. CT angiography shows occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery. Diagnosis: embolic ischemic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory from atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Emboli from the left atrium can travel to any branch of the cerebral circulation. If the embolus had instead lodged in the left posterior cerebral artery, which of the following deficits would be most likely?
options: Weakness of the right leg greater than the right arm
Pure motor weakness of the right face, arm, and leg
Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Loss of pain and temperature sense on the left face
approach: Recall the main cortical territory of the posterior cerebral artery: the occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe.
A left occipital lesion removes the right visual field of both eyes, a right homonymous hemianopia.
Macular sparing occurs because the occipital pole often receives collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery.
questions.why: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus. Each occipital lobe receives information about the opposite half of the visual field from both eyes, so a left PCA infarct produces a right homonymous hemianopia. The macula is often spared because its cortical representation at the occipital pole has a dual supply from the MCA and PCA.
whyNot: Leg-predominant weakness is the anterior cerebral artery syndrome, because the leg area of the motor cortex lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere.
Pure motor hemiparesis is a lacunar syndrome from occlusion of a lenticulostriate artery supplying the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
Correct.
Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss comes from the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the lateral medulla, supplied by the PICA or vertebral artery.

questions.stem: A repeat CT scan 2 days later shows patchy areas of blood within the infarcted territory. Which of the following best explains why this change is more typical of his type of infarct than of a thrombotic infarct?
options: Reperfusion of injured vessels after the embolus breaks up
Rupture of a Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm in the infarct
Amyloid deposits weakening cortical arteriole walls
Venous outflow blocked by thrombus in a dural sinus
approach: Identify the change as hemorrhagic conversion of an ischemic infarct.
Recall that emboli often fragment and move distally, restoring flow to the area.
Blood returning into necrotic, leaky vessel walls leaks into the tissue, so embolic infarcts often turn hemorrhagic, while a fixed thrombus keeps the territory bloodless (pale infarct).
questions.why: Embolic infarcts are often hemorrhagic. The embolus lyses or breaks up and moves downstream, and blood flows back into vessels whose walls were damaged by ischemia. The blood leaks out and gives a petechial or confluent hemorrhagic infarct. A thrombus at an atherosclerotic plaque usually stays in place, so the infarct remains pale.
whyNot: Correct.

Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms form in small penetrating arteries in chronic hypertension and cause primary intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, not bleeding into an infarct.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes recurrent lobar hemorrhages in older adults, unrelated to an embolic infarct.
Dural sinus thrombosis can cause venous hemorrhagic infarcts, but this patient has an arterial occlusion proven on CT angiography.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion causing his language deficit?
options: Angular gyrus of the parietal lobe
Posterior superior temporal gyrus
Arcuate fasciculus
Posterior inferior frontal gyrus
approach: Classify the aphasia: speech is nonfluent and repetition is impaired, but comprehension is intact.
Nonfluent speech with good comprehension is Broca aphasia.
Broca area lies in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, supplied by the superior division of the MCA.
questions.why: Broca aphasia produces slow, effortful, telegraphic speech with poor repetition while comprehension is largely intact. The lesion is in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) of the dominant, usually left, hemisphere. It often comes with right face and arm weakness because the adjacent motor cortex is in the same MCA superior division territory.
whyNot: A dominant angular gyrus lesion causes Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion), not a nonfluent aphasia.
Wernicke area lesions give fluent speech with poor comprehension, the opposite of this patient.
Damage to the arcuate fasciculus causes conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension with poor repetition.
Correct.

questions.stem: His right face and arm are much weaker than his right leg. Which of the following best explains this pattern of weakness?
options: Leg fibers cross in the pons, unlike arm fibers
The leg area of the precentral gyrus lies on the medial surface
The leg is represented mainly in the postcentral gyrus
Leg motor fibers run in the anterior limb of the internal capsule
approach: Recall the motor homunculus on the precentral gyrus: face and hand on the lateral convexity, leg on the medial surface.
The MCA supplies the lateral convexity; the ACA supplies the medial surface.
An MCA infarct therefore weakens the face and arm more than the leg.
questions.why: The primary motor cortex lies in the precentral gyrus. Its face, hand, and arm areas are on the lateral surface of the hemisphere, and the leg and foot area wraps over onto the medial surface in the paracentral lobule. The MCA supplies the lateral surface, so an MCA infarct causes contralateral face and arm weakness with relative sparing of the leg.
whyNot: All lateral corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, not in the pons.
Correct.
The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex. Its lesion causes loss of sensation, not weakness.
Corticospinal fibers for the arm and leg run in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The anterior limb carries mainly frontal and thalamic connections.

dx: Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage of the right putamen and internal capsule
case: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of headache, vomiting, and weakness of her left side while gardening. She has a 15-year history of hypertension and stopped taking her medications 6 months ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 212/118 mm Hg. She is drowsy but arousable. Physical examination shows left lower facial weakness, 2/5 strength in the left arm and leg, decreased sensation on the entire left side, and an extensor plantar response on the left. Her eyes are deviated to the right. A noncontrast CT scan of the head shows a 3.5-cm hyperdense hematoma in the right putamen extending into the internal capsule. Diagnosis: hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Which of the following vascular changes most likely preceded the rupture?
options: Amyloid beta deposition in cortical arteriole walls
Microaneurysms of small penetrating arteries
Saccular aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis
Direct artery-to-vein connections without a capillary bed
approach: Note the setting: chronic uncontrolled hypertension and a deep hemorrhage in the putamen.
Recall that chronic hypertension damages small penetrating arteries and forms Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms.
These vessels supply the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, the classic sites of hypertensive hemorrhage.
questions.why: Long-standing hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis and weakening of small penetrating arteries such as the lenticulostriates. Tiny Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms form and can rupture, producing a deep hematoma. The putamen is the most common site, followed by the thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.
whyNot: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhages near the cortex in older adults, not deep basal ganglia bleeds.
Correct.
A ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm bleeds mainly into the subarachnoid space, with sudden severe headache and blood in the basal cisterns.
Arteriovenous malformations can bleed into the brain, but they usually present in young adults with hemorrhage or seizures and are not caused by hypertension.

questions.stem: Her left hemiparesis results from damage to corticospinal fibers in the posterior limb of the right internal capsule. Which of the following best describes the course most of these fibers normally take after leaving the internal capsule?
options: Cerebral peduncle, then decussation in the midbrain tegmentum
Middle cerebellar peduncle, then decussation in the pons
Uncrossed descent in the anterior funiculus to the lumbar cord
Cerebral peduncle, then decussation in the caudal medulla
approach: Follow the corticospinal tract downward: internal capsule, cerebral peduncle in the midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramid.
About 85 to 90 percent of the fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
A lesion above the decussation therefore causes contralateral weakness.
questions.why: Corticospinal axons leave the precentral gyrus, pass through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, and descend in the middle portion of the cerebral peduncle and the basis pontis to the medullary pyramid. Most cross in the pyramidal decussation at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord and descend in the lateral corticospinal tract to anterior horn alpha motor neurons. Because the crossing is low, a right capsular lesion causes left-sided upper motor neuron weakness.
whyNot: The fibers pass through the cerebral peduncle, but they do not cross in the midbrain.
The middle cerebellar peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibers to the cerebellum, not corticospinal fibers.
The anterior corticospinal tract stays uncrossed in the anterior funiculus, but it carries only a small fraction of fibers and ends mainly in the cervical and upper thoracic cord.
Correct.

questions.stem: MRI 1 week later shows that the hemorrhage also disrupted white matter connections of the right inferior parietal lobule. She ignores people standing on her left, eats only from the right side of her plate, and denies that her left arm is weak. Which of the following best explains why this deficit follows right-sided rather than left-sided damage?
options: The right parietal lobe attends to both sides of space
The right parietal lobe holds the dominant language network
The right optic radiation carries both visual fields
The right somatosensory cortex receives bilateral input
approach: Recognize the behavior as hemispatial neglect with anosognosia (denial of the deficit).
Recall that the right parietal association cortex directs attention to both the left and right halves of space, while the left mainly attends to the right.
After a right-sided lesion, nothing attends to left space, so the left side is ignored.
questions.why: Spatial attention is lateralized. The nondominant (usually right) parietal association cortex attends to both hemispaces, while the left parietal lobe covers mainly the right hemispace. A right parietal lesion leaves the left side of space without attention, causing hemispatial neglect. A left parietal lesion is compensated by the intact right side, so neglect after left-sided damage is rare and mild.
whyNot: Correct.
Language is lateralized to the left hemisphere in almost all right-handed people. A dominant parietal lesion at the angular gyrus causes Gerstmann syndrome, not neglect.
Each optic radiation carries the opposite visual field only. Neglect also occurs when visual fields are intact.
Primary somatosensory cortex receives input from the opposite side of the body. A lesion there causes sensory loss, not inattention to one side of space.

questions.stem: In patients with sudden focal deficits, a noncontrast CT scan of the head is obtained before any thrombolytic therapy is considered. Which of the following best explains why this study is used first?
options: It shows ischemic infarcts within the first hour
It identifies the occluded artery and its collaterals
Acute blood is hyperdense without contrast
It maps the ischemic penumbra that can still be saved
approach: Recall that ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes can look identical at the bedside.
Thrombolysis is dangerous if the stroke is hemorrhagic.
Fresh blood is bright (hyperdense) on CT right away, while early ischemia is often invisible for hours.
questions.why: Ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and even TIA can present with the same sudden focal deficits, and they share risk factors such as hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, and dyslipidemia. Treatment differs completely, and thrombolytics would worsen a hemorrhage. Acute blood is dense and appears bright on a noncontrast CT within minutes, so this fast test reliably excludes hemorrhage before treatment.
whyNot: Early ischemic infarcts are often invisible on CT for the first several hours. MRI diffusion imaging detects them much sooner.
Locating the occluded vessel requires CT angiography or another vascular study, not a noncontrast scan.
Correct.
The penumbra is assessed with perfusion imaging (CT or MRI perfusion), not a plain noncontrast scan.

dx: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
case: A 44-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of the worst headache of her life while lifting weights. She briefly lost consciousness and has vomited twice. She has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 178/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows nuchal rigidity and photophobia. She is oriented, and there are no focal neurologic deficits. A noncontrast CT scan of the head shows blood in the basal cisterns and the anterior interhemispheric fissure. CT angiography shows a 7-mm saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery. Diagnosis: subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the formation of this type of aneurysm?
options: Atherosclerotic thinning along a long arterial segment
Septic emboli lodging in and weakening the vessel wall
Hyaline thickening of small penetrating arterioles
Weak tunica media at arterial branch points
approach: Identify the lesion as a saccular (berry) aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis.
Recall that the arterial wall at branch points has a deficient media and internal elastic lamina.
Link her ADPKD to the higher risk of saccular aneurysms; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, hypertension, and smoking also raise the risk.
questions.why: Saccular aneurysms form at branch points of the circle of Willis, most often near the anterior communicating artery, where the tunica media is thin or absent. Hemodynamic stress over years bulges the weak wall outward. ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome raise the risk, and hypertension and smoking add to it. Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with sudden severe headache.
whyNot: Atherosclerosis produces fusiform aneurysms, most often of the basilar artery, not small berry aneurysms at branch points.
Septic emboli from infective endocarditis cause mycotic aneurysms, usually in distal MCA branches. She has no signs of infection.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of penetrating arterioles leads to lacunar infarcts and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, which bleed into deep brain tissue.
Correct.

questions.stem: The parent vessel of her aneurysm links the two arteries that supply which of the following regions?
options: Occipital cortex and the inferior temporal lobe
Medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the leg area
Lateral convexity of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes
Internal capsule, basal ganglia, and thalamus
approach: Recall that the anterior communicating artery joins the right and left anterior cerebral arteries.
Recall the ACA territory: the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes.
That territory includes the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex.
questions.why: The circle of Willis connects the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. The anterior communicating artery joins the two anterior cerebral arteries, and the posterior communicating arteries join each internal carotid to a posterior cerebral artery. The ACAs run in the interhemispheric fissure and supply the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the leg region of the motor and sensory strips. This is why vasospasm after an ACom aneurysm rupture can cause leg weakness.
whyNot: The occipital and inferior temporal cortex belong to the posterior cerebral arteries, which come from the basilar artery.
Correct.
The lateral convexity is the middle cerebral artery territory. The MCAs are not joined by a communicating artery.
The internal capsule and basal ganglia are supplied mainly by lenticulostriate branches of the MCA, and the thalamus by small PCA branches.

questions.stem: Arteriovenous malformations are another common cause of intracranial bleeding in young adults. Which of the following angiographic findings would indicate an arteriovenous malformation rather than an aneurysm?
options: A rounded outpouching at an arterial branch point
A spindle-shaped dilation of a long arterial segment
Early venous filling through a tangle of vessels
Beaded narrowing of the internal carotid arteries
approach: Recall the defining structure of an AVM: arteries draining directly into veins with no capillary bed.
Without capillary resistance, contrast reaches the veins during the arterial phase.
Pick the finding of early venous filling through a vascular tangle.
questions.why: An arteriovenous malformation is a tangle (nidus) of abnormal vessels in which arteries connect directly to veins without an intervening capillary bed. Blood shunts through at high flow and pressure, so draining veins fill early on angiography and their thin walls can rupture. AVMs typically present in young adults with intracerebral hemorrhage or seizures.
whyNot: A rounded outpouching at a branch point is a saccular aneurysm, the lesion in this patient.
A spindle-shaped dilation is a fusiform aneurysm, usually atherosclerotic.
Correct.
A string-of-beads pattern is typical of fibromuscular dysplasia, which narrows rather than shunts vessels.

questions.stem: If her CT scan had been normal, a lumbar puncture 12 hours after onset would have been the next step. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings would be most likely?
options: Xanthochromia with a constant red cell count
Clear fluid with lymphocytes and normal glucose
Turbid fluid with neutrophils and low glucose
Clear fluid with high protein and few cells
approach: Recall that subarachnoid hemorrhage puts red cells directly into the CSF.
Red cells lyse over hours and release hemoglobin, which is broken down to bilirubin, giving a yellow tint (xanthochromia).
A traumatic tap shows red cells that fall from tube 1 to tube 4 and no xanthochromia; SAH shows a steady count.
questions.why: In subarachnoid hemorrhage the CSF contains many red cells in every tube collected. Over the first hours, red cells lyse and release hemoglobin, which is converted to bilirubin. By about 12 hours the supernatant is reliably yellow (xanthochromia). A traumatic tap shows a falling red cell count across tubes and a clear supernatant. Opening pressure is often raised, and protein rises slightly from the blood.
whyNot: Correct.
Clear CSF with lymphocytes and normal glucose is the pattern of viral meningitis.
Turbid CSF with neutrophils and low glucose is the pattern of bacterial meningitis.
High protein with few cells (albuminocytologic dissociation) is typical of Guillain-Barre syndrome.

dx: Epidural hematoma from a temporal bone fracture with uncal herniation
case: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after he was struck on the left side of the head by a baseball. He lost consciousness briefly, then talked normally. Over the past hour, he has developed a severe headache, vomiting, and increasing drowsiness. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 54/min, respirations are 10/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 182/96 mm Hg. He opens his eyes only to pain. The left pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light; the right pupil is 3 mm and reactive. He has right-sided weakness and a right extensor plantar response. CT of the head shows a biconvex hyperdense collection over the left temporal lobe that does not cross sutures, a left squamous temporal bone fracture, and midline shift. Diagnosis: epidural hematoma with uncal herniation.

questions.stem: The fracture line crosses the thin bone at the pterion. Laceration of which of the following vessels is the most likely source of the hematoma?
options: Middle meningeal artery
Bridging cortical veins
Superior sagittal sinus
Middle cerebral artery
approach: Note the clues: temporal bone fracture, lucid interval, and a biconvex collection limited by sutures.
These describe an epidural hematoma, which forms between the skull and the periosteal dura.
The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner table under the pterion and tears with the fracture.
questions.why: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and runs between the dura and the inner table beneath the pterion, where the bone is thin. A temporal fracture tears it, and arterial blood strips the dura from the skull. The dura is attached firmly at sutures, so the collection is biconvex and does not cross suture lines. Arterial pressure makes it expand quickly after a lucid interval.
whyNot: Correct.
Torn bridging veins cause a subdural hematoma, which is crescent shaped and crosses suture lines.
The superior sagittal sinus runs in the midline, far from a temporal fracture. Sinus tears can cause epidural bleeding at the vertex, but not here.
The middle cerebral artery lies in the subarachnoid space. Its rupture would not collect blood between the dura and skull.

questions.stem: The medial temporal lobe has been pushed past the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli. As this herniation progresses, which of the following arteries is most likely to be compressed?
options: Anterior cerebral artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery
approach: Identify uncal (transtentorial) herniation of the medial temporal lobe through the tentorial notch.
List the structures at the tentorial notch: CN III, the cerebral peduncle, and the posterior cerebral artery.
PCA compression can cause an occipital infarct.
questions.why: In uncal herniation the uncus of the temporal lobe slides medially and downward through the tentorial notch. There it compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (dilated pupil), the cerebral peduncle, and the posterior cerebral artery as it curves around the midbrain. PCA compression can infarct the occipital lobe and cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia in survivors.
whyNot: The anterior cerebral artery is compressed against the falx cerebri in subfalcine (cingulate) herniation.
The posterior inferior cerebellar artery runs beside the medulla, far below the tentorial notch. The danger there comes from tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum.
Correct.
The middle cerebral artery runs in the lateral sulcus and is not trapped at the tentorial notch.

questions.stem: When a bright light is shone into his left eye, which of the following responses is expected?
options: Neither of the pupils constricts
Only the right pupil constricts
Only the left pupil constricts
Both pupils constrict normally
approach: Separate the two limbs of the reflex: CN II carries light information in, and CN III carries the constriction signal out.
Uncal herniation compresses the left CN III, so the efferent limb to the left pupil is lost while the left optic nerve still works.
Light in the left eye reaches both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so the right pupil constricts (consensual response) and the left does not.
questions.why: Light entering one eye travels in CN II to the pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Parasympathetic fibers then travel in each CN III to the ciliary ganglion and the pupillary sphincter. With the left CN III compressed, the afferent signal from the left eye is still received, so the right pupil constricts, but the left pupil cannot constrict in response to light in either eye.
whyNot: Loss of both responses would require a lesion of the left optic nerve or both efferent pathways. His right CN III is intact.
Correct.
This would occur with a right CN III lesion, the opposite side from his herniation.
Both pupils constricting normally means both pathways work, which does not fit a fixed, dilated left pupil.

questions.stem: If the hematoma is not evacuated and the brainstem continues to shift downward, which of the following is the most likely finding at autopsy?
options: Hemorrhagic conversion of a cerebellar infarct
Blood filling the ventricles from the hematoma
Hydrocephalus from blocked arachnoid granulations
Pontine hemorrhages from torn basilar branches
approach: Follow the sequence: expanding hematoma, rising intracranial pressure, uncal herniation, downward brainstem displacement.
The basilar artery is tethered, so its small paramedian branches stretch and tear as the brainstem moves down.
This produces secondary (Duret) hemorrhages in the midbrain and pons, which are usually fatal.
questions.why: An expanding epidural hematoma raises intracranial pressure until the uncus herniates. Continued pressure pushes the brainstem downward while the basilar artery stays relatively fixed, so its paramedian perforating branches stretch and rupture. The resulting Duret hemorrhages in the midline midbrain and pons destroy vital centers and cause death unless the hematoma is removed promptly.
whyNot: A cerebellar infarct is not part of this process, and hemorrhagic conversion follows reperfusion of an ischemic infarct.
An epidural hematoma lies outside the dura, so it cannot spread into the ventricles.
Blocked arachnoid granulations cause communicating hydrocephalus after subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis, a slower process.
Correct.

dx: Acute subdural hematoma with contrecoup frontal contusions after a fall
case: An 81-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after he slipped and fell backward, striking the back of his head on a tile floor. He was initially confused, and over the next few hours he became increasingly difficult to arouse. He drinks about six beers daily. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 168/88 mm Hg. He opens his eyes only to pain and withdraws his limbs from painful stimuli. There is a large occipital scalp hematoma. A CT scan of the head shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the left frontoparietal convexity that crosses the coronal suture, with 7 mm of midline shift, contusions of both frontal poles and the inferior frontal lobes, and diffuse cerebral atrophy. Diagnosis: acute subdural hematoma with contrecoup frontal contusions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why older adults with brain atrophy are at increased risk for this type of hematoma?
options: Thinning of the squamous temporal bone over the pterion
Hyaline thickening of small penetrating arterioles
Stretching of veins crossing from cortex to dural sinus
Loss of CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations
approach: Identify the lesion: a crescent-shaped collection crossing sutures is a subdural hematoma.
Recall the source: bridging veins that run from the cortical surface across the subdural space to the dural venous sinuses.
Atrophy pulls the brain away from the skull, stretching these veins so minor trauma tears them.
questions.why: Cortical veins drain into the dural venous sinuses, such as the superior sagittal sinus, by crossing the subdural space as bridging veins. Blood then leaves through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular veins. When the brain shrinks with age or chronic alcohol use, these bridging veins are stretched and tear easily with acceleration-deceleration forces. Venous blood spreads along the convexity under the dura and crosses suture lines.
whyNot: A thin pterion predisposes to middle meningeal artery tears and epidural hematoma, not subdural bleeding.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of penetrating arterioles causes lacunar infarcts and deep hypertensive hemorrhage.
Correct.
Impaired CSF absorption causes communicating hydrocephalus, not bleeding.

questions.stem: He struck the back of his head, yet his contusions are in the frontal lobes. Which of the following best explains the location of the contusions?
options: Rupture of small arteries beneath the scalp hematoma
Shearing of long axons at the gray-white junction
Spread of subdural blood into the frontal cortex
Brain striking the inner skull opposite the impact
approach: Recall that a moving head that stops suddenly lets the brain keep moving inside the skull.
A coup injury forms at the impact site; a contrecoup injury forms on the opposite side as the brain hits the skull there.
The frontal and temporal poles rest on rough bony floors, so they bruise most often.
questions.why: When the moving head strikes a fixed surface, the brain continues forward and then rebounds within the skull. The surface opposite the impact strikes the inner table, producing a contrecoup contusion. Contusions are most common at the frontal poles, orbital frontal surfaces, and temporal poles because these areas lie against irregular bony ridges of the anterior and middle cranial fossae.
whyNot: Scalp vessels are outside the skull. A scalp hematoma does not bruise brain tissue.
Shearing of axons is diffuse axonal injury. It causes coma with axonal swellings at the gray-white junction and corpus callosum, not focal cortical bruises.
Subdural blood compresses the brain surface but does not infiltrate the cortex to form contusions.
Correct.

questions.stem: His hematoma involves only one cerebral hemisphere. Which of the following best explains his depressed level of consciousness?
options: Compression of the upper brainstem reticular formation
Injury limited to the left primary motor cortex and its fibers
Damage to the hippocampus of the left temporal lobe
Pressure on the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis
approach: Recall that consciousness requires the ascending reticular activating system of the upper pons and midbrain plus at least one working cerebral hemisphere.
A lesion in one hemisphere alone does not cause coma.
A mass lesion causes coma when shift and herniation compress the upper brainstem and diencephalon.
questions.why: Arousal depends on the ascending reticular activating system in the upper pons and midbrain, which projects through the thalamus to both hemispheres. Coma results from damage to this system or from widespread dysfunction of both hemispheres. A unilateral subdural hematoma causes coma when midline shift and herniation compress the upper brainstem. Brain death differs from coma: it is irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function, including brainstem reflexes and respiratory drive.
whyNot: Correct.
A primary motor cortex lesion causes contralateral weakness, not loss of consciousness.
Damage to one hippocampus impairs memory formation but does not reduce arousal.
Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia. Coma occurs only if a cerebellar mass compresses the brainstem.

questions.stem: His daughter reports that he boxed professionally for 15 years and has had slowly worsening memory, irritability, and unsteady gait for several years before this fall. Which of the following would most likely be found in his brain?
options: Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in substantia nigra neurons
Perivascular tau tangles at the depths of sulci
Spongiform change from misfolded prion protein
TDP-43 inclusions in anterior horn motor neurons
approach: Link years of repeated head impacts with progressive cognitive and behavioral decline.
This is chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica).
Its marker is hyperphosphorylated tau, typically around small vessels at the depths of cortical sulci.
questions.why: Repeated concussive and subconcussive blows can lead to chronic traumatic encephalopathy. A single concussion causes transient dysfunction with normal imaging and may leave postconcussion symptoms, but repeated injury over years causes progressive memory loss, mood and behavior change, and parkinsonian or gait features. Pathology shows hyperphosphorylated tau tangles clustered around small vessels at the depths of sulci, with brain atrophy.
whyNot: Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein in the substantia nigra define Parkinson disease. The marker of repeated head trauma is tau, not alpha-synuclein.
Correct.
Spongiform change from prion protein is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rapidly progressive dementia over months.
TDP-43 inclusions in motor neurons are typical of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

dx: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from vertebral artery dissection
case: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of sudden vertigo, nausea, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing that began 4 hours ago. Three days ago she was in a rear-end motor vehicle collision, and since then she has had pain in the right side of the back of her neck. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows right ptosis and miosis, nystagmus, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face and on the left trunk and limbs, right limb ataxia, and weakness of the right soft palate. Strength in all limbs is normal. MRI shows an infarct in the right lateral medulla. MR angiography shows a dissection of the right vertebral artery. Diagnosis: lateral medullary syndrome from vertebral artery dissection.

questions.stem: Damage to which of the following structures best explains the loss of pain and temperature sensation on her left trunk and limbs?
options: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract
Lateral spinothalamic tract
Medial lemniscus
Medullary pyramid
approach: Note the crossed sensory pattern: pain loss on the right face and the left body.
Pain fibers from the body cross in the spinal cord and ascend in the spinothalamic tract, which runs through the lateral medulla.
A right lateral medullary lesion therefore removes pain sensation from the left body.
questions.why: The lateral medulla, supplied by the PICA and the vertebral artery, contains the spinothalamic tract, the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, the nucleus ambiguus, the vestibular nuclei, the inferior cerebellar peduncle, and descending sympathetic fibers. Spinothalamic fibers have already crossed in the spinal cord, so a right lesion causes left body pain and temperature loss. The trigeminal pain fibers have not yet crossed, so the face loses sensation on the right. The medial structures (pyramid, medial lemniscus, CN XII) are spared, which is why her strength is normal.
whyNot: The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract carry pain from the ipsilateral face. Their damage explains her right facial sensory loss, not the left body loss.
Correct.
The medial lemniscus carries vibration and position sense and lies medially. It is damaged in medial medullary syndrome from anterior spinal artery occlusion.
The pyramid carries corticospinal fibers. Its damage causes contralateral weakness, which she does not have.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the arterial injury led to her infarct?
options: Intimal tear causing an intramural hematoma and thrombus
Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation
Reversed vertebral flow from proximal subclavian stenosis
Lipohyalinosis of small penetrating medullary arteries
approach: Note the setting: a young adult with neck pain after neck trauma, then a posterior circulation stroke.
Recall that dissection begins with a tear in the intima, letting blood track into the wall.
The intramural hematoma narrows the lumen, and thrombus at the tear can occlude the artery or embolize.
questions.why: Cervical artery dissection is a leading cause of stroke in young adults. Neck trauma, even minor, tears the intima, and blood enters the vessel wall to form an intramural hematoma. The lumen narrows, and thrombus forms on the exposed wall, which can occlude the vessel or send emboli downstream. Neck pain or headache on the side of the dissection often precedes the stroke. Carotid dissection classically adds an ipsilateral Horner syndrome from injury to the sympathetic plexus on the artery.
whyNot: Correct.
Carotid bifurcation plaque causes anterior circulation thrombotic or embolic strokes in older adults with atherosclerotic risk factors.
Subclavian steal reverses vertebral flow and causes arm claudication, unequal arm blood pressures, and transient vertebrobasilar symptoms with arm exercise, not dissection after trauma.
Lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries in hypertension causes small lacunar infarcts, not a dissection-related infarct in a young adult.

questions.stem: Her right ptosis and miosis result from interruption of which of the following neurons?
options: Postganglionic fibers in the internal carotid plexus
Preganglionic fibers leaving the T1 ventral root
Parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Descending hypothalamic fibers in the lateral brainstem
approach: Recognize Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, and often anhidrosis.
Trace the three-neuron path: hypothalamus down the lateral brainstem to C8 to T2, then to the superior cervical ganglion, then along the carotid plexus.
Her lesion is in the lateral medulla, so the first-order (central) neurons are interrupted.
questions.why: The oculosympathetic pathway has three neurons. First-order neurons descend from the hypothalamus through the lateral brainstem and cervical cord to the ciliospinal center at C8 to T2. Second-order preganglionic neurons exit the upper thoracic roots and ascend over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion. Third-order postganglionic fibers travel on the internal carotid artery to the dilator pupillae and the superior tarsal muscle. A lateral medullary infarct interrupts the first-order fibers and causes an ipsilateral central Horner syndrome.
whyNot: Postganglionic fibers on the internal carotid artery are injured in carotid dissection, not in a medullary infarct.
Preganglionic fibers at T1 are injured by a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex.
Loss of Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic output causes a dilated pupil, the opposite of miosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her vertigo and nystagmus result from damage to the right vestibular nuclei. Which of the following best explains why a one-sided lesion produces a false sense of rotation?
options: Loss of linear acceleration signals from both utricles
Increased firing of the damaged nuclei during head turns
Unequal tonic input from the two vestibular sides
Loss of cochlear input from the ipsilateral ear
approach: Recall that each vestibular apparatus fires tonically at rest, and the brain compares the two sides.
Head rotation normally raises firing on one side and lowers it on the other.
A one-sided loss mimics this imbalance, so the brain senses rotation and the vestibulo-ocular reflex drives nystagmus.
questions.why: The semicircular canals sense angular acceleration, and the utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration and gravity. Both sides fire at a steady rate at rest. Turning the head increases firing on one side and decreases it on the other, and the brain reads this difference as rotation. When one side's vestibular nuclei are damaged, the resulting imbalance is read as constant rotation, producing vertigo, and the vestibulo-ocular reflex drives the eyes slowly to one side with corrective fast phases (nystagmus).
whyNot: The utricles signal linear acceleration and head tilt, not rotation, and a one-sided lesion does not remove input from both.
Damaged nuclei fire less, not more. The symptom comes from the imbalance between the two sides.
Correct.
Cochlear input carries hearing. Its loss causes deafness, as in AICA infarcts, but not vertigo.

dx: Global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy after cardiac arrest
case: A 57-year-old man collapses while exercising at a gym. An automated external defibrillator shows ventricular fibrillation, and a return of spontaneous circulation is achieved after 22 minutes of resuscitation. During the next 24 hours, his systolic blood pressure repeatedly falls below 80 mm Hg. On day 5, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min on a ventilator, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. He does not open his eyes or respond to commands. Pupils react to light, and he has intermittent generalized myoclonic jerks. MRI of the brain shows restricted diffusion in the cerebral cortex, both hippocampi, and the border zones between the anterior and middle cerebral artery territories. Diagnosis: global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. He dies on day 9.

questions.stem: At autopsy, which of the following neuronal populations is most likely to show the most severe loss?
options: Granule cells of the hippocampal dentate gyrus
Motor neurons of the brainstem cranial nerve nuclei
Motor neurons of the spinal cord anterior horns
Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampal CA1 sector
approach: Recall that neurons differ in their sensitivity to global hypoxia.
The most vulnerable are hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, and pyramidal neurons of neocortical layers 3, 5, and 6.
Brainstem and spinal cord neurons are relatively resistant.
questions.why: Global hypoxia-ischemia damages neurons selectively. Hippocampal CA1 (Sommer sector) pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, and neocortical pyramidal neurons are most vulnerable, in part because of high glutamate receptor density and high energy demand. Cortical damage produces laminar necrosis. Severe hypotension also causes watershed infarcts in border zones between arterial territories, as seen on his MRI.
whyNot: Dentate granule cells lie in the same hippocampal formation but are relatively resistant to hypoxia.
Brainstem motor neurons are relatively resistant, which is why brainstem reflexes such as the pupillary response can persist after severe cortical injury.
Spinal anterior horn cells are relatively resistant to global hypoxia.
Correct.

questions.stem: Sections of the cerebral cortex show many neurons with shrunken cell bodies, intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm, and small dark pyknotic nuclei. Which of the following best describes these cells?
options: Reversible injury that began within minutes of arrest
Reactive gliosis from injury several weeks old
Irreversible injury at least 12 to 24 hours old
Chromatolysis from injury to the neuron's own axon
approach: Identify the cells as red neurons from the shrinkage, eosinophilia, and pyknosis.
Red neurons mark irreversible neuronal death.
They first appear about 12 to 24 hours after hypoxia or ischemia.
questions.why: Red neurons are the earliest reliable histologic sign of irreversible neuronal injury. The cell body shrinks, the cytoplasm turns intensely eosinophilic as Nissl substance is lost, and the nucleus becomes pyknotic. They appear about 12 to 24 hours after the hypoxic or ischemic event, so their presence shows the injury is permanent and at least that old.
whyNot: Reversible injury in the first minutes to hours shows little or no change on light microscopy.
Reactive gliosis is an astrocyte response that becomes prominent over weeks. It describes glial cells, not shrunken neurons.
Correct.
Chromatolysis after axonal injury shows a swollen cell body with dispersed Nissl substance and a nucleus pushed to the edge, the opposite appearance.

questions.stem: On day 3, while he is receiving an insulin infusion and his tube feeding is interrupted, serum glucose falls to 38 mg/dL (reference 70 to 100 mg/dL), and he has a generalized seizure. Which of the following best explains why his brain cannot compensate for the low glucose?
options: Neuronal glucose uptake depends on insulin through GLUT4
The brain cannot use fatty acids and has little glycogen
Glucose crosses the blood-brain barrier by simple diffusion
Neuronal GLUT3 has too low an affinity to take up glucose
approach: Recall how glucose reaches neurons: GLUT1 across the blood-brain barrier and GLUT3 on neurons, both independent of insulin.
Ask what fuel the brain can use when glucose is low: it cannot oxidize fatty acids, and its glycogen store is tiny.
Ketone bodies can substitute only after days of fasting, so acute hypoglycemia causes neuroglycopenia.
questions.why: The brain depends almost entirely on blood glucose. Glucose crosses the blood-brain barrier through GLUT1 and enters neurons through high-affinity GLUT3, neither of which needs insulin. The brain does not use fatty acids as a fuel, and its glycogen store (mostly in astrocytes) lasts only minutes. Ketone bodies become a major fuel only after several days of fasting. Acute hypoglycemia therefore causes neuroglycopenic symptoms: confusion, seizures, and coma.
whyNot: GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent transporter in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Neuronal glucose uptake does not depend on insulin.
Correct.
Glucose is too polar to diffuse across the barrier. It needs facilitated transport through GLUT1.
GLUT3 has a high affinity for glucose, which helps neurons take up glucose even at modestly low levels.

questions.stem: During the arrest, ATP in his neurons fell within minutes. Which of the following best explains the resulting loss of the neuronal resting membrane potential?
options: Pump failure with a rise in extracellular K+
A fall in the extracellular K+ concentration
Increased Cl- entry through GABA-A channels
Loss of voltage-gated Na+ channel function
approach: Recall that the resting potential is set mainly by K+ leak channels and the K+ gradient, which the Na+/K+ ATPase maintains.
Without ATP the pump stops, K+ leaks out and builds up outside cells, and Na+ accumulates inside.
By the Nernst equation, higher extracellular K+ makes the K+ equilibrium potential less negative, so the membrane depolarizes.
questions.why: The resting membrane potential, about -70 mV in neurons, is close to the K+ equilibrium potential because K+ leak channels dominate at rest. The Na+/K+ ATPase keeps K+ high inside and low outside. When ATP is lost, the pump fails, K+ accumulates in the extracellular space, and the Nernst potential for K+ shifts toward zero. The neurons depolarize, release glutamate, and enter a cycle of calcium overload and cell death.
whyNot: Correct.
A fall in extracellular K+ would make the K+ equilibrium potential more negative and hyperpolarize the cell.
Chloride entry through GABA-A channels makes the inside more negative and hyperpolarizes the cell.
Voltage-gated Na+ channels generate action potentials. They contribute little to the resting potential, so their loss would not depolarize the cell.

dx: Anterior spinal artery syndrome after thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair
case: A 68-year-old woman undergoes open repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm that requires prolonged aortic cross-clamping. When she awakens 6 hours later, she cannot move her legs. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows flaccid paralysis of both legs with absent patellar and Achilles reflexes. Pain and temperature sensation are absent below the level of the umbilicus, but vibration and joint position sense in the toes are normal. She has urinary retention requiring a catheter. MRI of the spine shows increased T2 signal in the anterior two thirds of the spinal cord from T8 to T11. Diagnosis: anterior spinal artery syndrome.

questions.stem: Loss of flow from which of the following arteries most likely caused her cord infarct?
options: Artery of Adamkiewicz
Posterior spinal artery
Intracranial vertebral artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
approach: Note the pattern: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature, with vibration and position sense spared. This is the anterior two thirds of the cord.
The anterior spinal artery supplies that region, and in the lower thoracic cord it depends on the artery of Adamkiewicz.
This radicular artery usually arises from a lower intercostal or upper lumbar branch of the aorta, so aortic clamping or repair can cut off its flow.
questions.why: The spinal cord has one anterior spinal artery supplying the anterior two thirds and two posterior spinal arteries supplying the dorsal columns. Along most of the thoracic cord, the anterior spinal artery is reinforced by few radicular feeders. The largest, the artery of Adamkiewicz, usually arises from the aorta between about T9 and T12 on the left. Aortic surgery or dissection can interrupt it, infarcting the anterior cord while the dorsal columns are spared.
whyNot: Correct.
Posterior spinal artery infarction damages the dorsal columns and would remove vibration and position sense, which she has kept.
The vertebral arteries form the anterior spinal artery at the medulla and feed the upper cervical cord, not the lower thoracic cord.
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut. Its loss causes colonic ischemia, not cord infarction.

questions.stem: Her urinary retention reflects loss of descending control over the pathway that contracts the detrusor muscle during voiding. Which of the following best describes the motor innervation of the detrusor?
options: One anterior horn neuron releasing ACh on nicotinic receptors
Two neurons, the second releasing norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptors
One sacral neuron releasing ACh directly on muscarinic receptors
Two neurons, the second releasing ACh on muscarinic receptors
approach: Identify the detrusor as smooth muscle, so its motor supply is visceral (autonomic), not somatic.
Visceral motor pathways use two neurons: a preganglionic neuron in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron in a ganglion.
Detrusor contraction is parasympathetic: S2 to S4 preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia near the bladder, and postganglionic fibers release ACh on M3 receptors.
questions.why: Somatic motor control uses one neuron: an anterior horn alpha motor neuron releasing acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle, such as the external urethral sphincter. Visceral motor control of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands uses two neurons. For the detrusor, parasympathetic preganglionic neurons at S2 to S4 travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves to ganglia in or near the bladder wall, and postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine on muscarinic (M3) receptors to contract the bladder.
whyNot: This is the somatic pathway to skeletal muscle, such as the external urethral sphincter supplied by the pudendal nerve.
Sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptors to contract the internal urethral sphincter and help store urine, not to empty the bladder.
Visceral motor pathways always use two neurons. No CNS neuron projects directly onto smooth muscle.
Correct.

questions.stem: She dies of a pulmonary embolism 10 days after surgery. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in the infarcted segment of the cord?
options: Red neurons with no inflammatory cells
Foamy macrophages in softened necrotic tissue
Dense sheets of neutrophils in the gray matter
A fluid-filled cavity walled off by dense gliosis
approach: Recall the time course of CNS infarction: red neurons at 12 to 24 hours, neutrophils in the first few days, macrophages over the following weeks, then gliosis and a cyst.
At 10 days, liquefactive necrosis is under way and macrophages are clearing lipid-rich myelin debris.
Pick foamy (lipid-laden) macrophages.
questions.why: CNS infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis. Red neurons appear at about 12 to 24 hours, neutrophils infiltrate during the first few days, and by about the end of the first week macrophages (microglia and blood monocytes) become the main cells, filling with lipid from broken-down myelin. Over the following weeks and months, astrocytes form a glial scar around a fluid-filled cyst.
whyNot: Red neurons without inflammation describe the first day after the infarct.
Correct.
Neutrophils predominate during roughly the first 1 to 3 days, not at 10 days.
A cavity lined by gliosis is the end stage, seen weeks to months after the infarct.

questions.stem: Had she survived, her leg tone would be expected to increase and her patellar reflexes to become brisk over the following weeks. Which of the following best describes the circuit of the patellar reflex?
options: Golgi tendon organ, Ib afferent, inhibitory interneuron
Muscle spindle, Ia afferent, interneuron, gamma motor neuron
Muscle spindle, Ia afferent, direct synapse on alpha motor neuron
Free nerve ending, A-delta afferent, interneurons, flexor motor neurons
approach: Recall that tapping the tendon stretches the quadriceps and its muscle spindles.
The spindle's Ia afferent synapses directly (one synapse) on alpha motor neurons to the same muscle.
The patellar reflex uses the L4 segment, below her lesion, so the arc is intact and becomes brisk once descending inhibition is lost.
questions.why: The stretch (myotatic) reflex is monosynaptic. Stretch of muscle spindles excites Ia afferents, which synapse directly on alpha motor neurons of the same muscle and cause it to contract. The patellar reflex is mainly L4, the biceps C5, the triceps C7, and the Achilles S1. After a thoracic cord lesion, the reflex arcs below the lesion survive, and once spinal shock resolves the loss of descending inhibition makes them hyperactive.
whyNot: The Golgi tendon organ Ib reflex senses tension and inhibits the same muscle, the opposite of a reflex jerk.
Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity but are not the efferent limb of the stretch reflex, and the reflex has no interneuron.
Correct.
Free nerve endings and A-delta fibers drive the polysynaptic withdrawal reflex to painful stimuli.

case: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her son because of a 3-year history of progressive forgetfulness. She repeats the same questions during conversations, misplaces items, and recently got lost while driving in her own neighborhood. Over the past 6 months, she has been unable to manage her bills. She clearly recalls events from her childhood. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no tremor, rigidity, or gait abnormality. She scores 19 of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination (normal 24 or higher). Serum vitamin B12 and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels are within the reference ranges. MRI of the brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy, most marked in the medial temporal lobes, with enlarged lateral ventricles and widened sulci. Diagnosis: Alzheimer disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences of enzyme cleavage of amyloid precursor protein produces the main component of the extracellular plaques in her brain?
options: Alpha secretase, then gamma secretase
Alpha secretase, then beta secretase
Beta secretase, then gamma secretase
Gamma secretase, then alpha secretase
approach: Identify the plaque protein as amyloid beta, a fragment of amyloid precursor protein.
Recall the two processing routes: alpha secretase cuts inside the amyloid beta sequence and prevents its formation; beta secretase does not.
Beta secretase cleavage followed by gamma secretase cleavage releases amyloid beta.
questions.why: Amyloid precursor protein is a transmembrane protein encoded on chromosome 21. Normally, alpha secretase cleaves it within the amyloid beta region, which prevents amyloid beta from forming. In the amyloidogenic pathway, beta secretase cuts first, then gamma secretase (which contains presenilin) cuts within the membrane, releasing amyloid beta that aggregates into plaques. Risk rises with age, APOE e4, Down syndrome (an extra APP gene copy), and mutations in APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2.
whyNot: This is the normal, nonamyloidogenic pathway. Alpha secretase cuts through the amyloid beta sequence.
Alpha secretase cleavage destroys the amyloid beta sequence, and this order does not occur.
Correct.
Gamma secretase acts on the membrane stub left after alpha or beta secretase, not first.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the enlargement of her lateral ventricles?
options: Obstruction of CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct
Filling of space left by lost brain tissue
Impaired CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations
Overproduction of CSF by the choroid plexus
approach: Note that the ventricles are enlarged together with widened sulci and cortical atrophy.
This is hydrocephalus ex vacuo: CSF fills the space left by neuron loss, and pressure is normal.
Her lack of gait problems also argues against normal pressure hydrocephalus.
questions.why: Alzheimer disease causes cortical atrophy with narrowed gyri, widened sulci, and compensatory enlargement of the ventricles (hydrocephalus ex vacuo). The atrophy is most marked in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, matching her early memory loss. Microscopy shows neuritic plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, and often amyloid angiopathy.
whyNot: Aqueductal obstruction causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles, raised pressure, and narrowed sulci.
Correct.
Impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations causes communicating hydrocephalus, including normal pressure hydrocephalus with gait disturbance and urinary incontinence.
CSF overproduction is rare, caused mainly by a choroid plexus papilloma, and is not linked to neurodegeneration.

topics: Gross and microscopic findings in Alzheimer disease

questions.stem: She is started on donepezil, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Which of the following enzymes and neuronal populations best match the transmitter deficit this drug addresses?
options: Tyrosine hydroxylase in the substantia nigra
Tryptophan hydroxylase in the raphe nuclei
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase in the locus coeruleus
Choline acetyltransferase in the nucleus basalis
approach: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor raises synaptic acetylcholine, so the deficit is cholinergic.
Acetylcholine is made from acetyl-CoA and choline by choline acetyltransferase.
The main cholinergic projection to the cortex comes from the nucleus basalis of Meynert, which degenerates early in Alzheimer disease.
questions.why: Choline acetyltransferase joins acetyl-CoA and choline to form acetylcholine, and acetylcholinesterase breaks it down to acetate and choline in the synaptic cleft. The nucleus basalis of Meynert in the basal forebrain sends cholinergic fibers throughout the cortex, and its neurons are lost early in Alzheimer disease. Blocking acetylcholinesterase prolongs the action of the acetylcholine that remains.
whyNot: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine. Loss of dopaminergic nigral neurons causes Parkinson disease.
Tryptophan hydroxylase makes serotonin in the raphe nuclei. Donepezil does not act on serotonin.
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase makes norepinephrine in the locus coeruleus. Donepezil does not act on norepinephrine.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her earliest symptom was an inability to retain new information, while memories from decades ago remained intact. Damage to which of the following structures best explains this pattern?
options: Hippocampal formation
Amygdala
Mammillary bodies
Anterior cingulate gyrus
approach: Classify the deficit: trouble forming new memories with old memories preserved is anterograde amnesia.
The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories, and remote memories are stored in the neocortex.
Her MRI shows medial temporal atrophy, where the hippocampus lies.
questions.why: The hippocampus is needed to convert new experiences into long-term declarative memories, but long-stored memories reside in the neocortex. Hippocampal damage therefore causes anterograde amnesia while remote memories are relatively preserved. In Alzheimer disease, neurofibrillary tangles and neuron loss begin in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, which is why short-term memory loss is the first symptom.
whyNot: Correct.
Bilateral amygdala damage causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome with hyperorality, hypersexuality, and loss of fear, not isolated memory loss.
Mammillary body damage occurs in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency. It is not the main site of damage in Alzheimer disease, and her MRI points to the medial temporal lobe.
The anterior cingulate gyrus is involved in emotion and motivation. Its damage causes apathy and reduced initiative, not anterograde amnesia.

case: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of progressive weakness. He first noticed he was dropping tools with his right hand, then his left leg became stiff, and over the past 2 months his speech has become slurred and he chokes on liquids. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the right hand, fasciculations in both arms and the tongue, and tongue atrophy. Muscle tone is increased in both legs. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk in all four limbs, including the atrophic right arm, and plantar responses are extensor bilaterally. Sensation, eye movements, and bladder function are normal. Electromyography shows active denervation with fasciculation potentials in the arms, legs, and tongue; sensory nerve conduction studies are normal. Diagnosis: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely in his spinal cord at autopsy?
options: Demyelinating plaques in the periventricular white matter
Loss of anterior horn cells with lateral column sclerosis
Degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal root ganglia
Cavitation of the central gray matter of the cervical cord
approach: Note the mix of lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations) and upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, Babinski) with normal sensation.
This means degeneration of both anterior horn cells and corticospinal neurons.
In the cord, this appears as loss of anterior horn cells and scarring (sclerosis) of the lateral corticospinal tracts.
questions.why: ALS destroys both upper and lower motor neurons. Anterior horn cells and brainstem motor neurons are lost, and degeneration of corticospinal axons leaves the lateral columns pale and gliotic, which gives the disease its name. Most cases are sporadic, and some familial cases carry SOD1 or C9orf72 mutations. Sensation, bladder control, and eye movements are usually spared, and most patients die of respiratory failure within a few years.
whyNot: Demyelinating plaques in periventricular white matter are the hallmark of multiple sclerosis, which causes sensory and visual symptoms, not fasciculations.
Correct.
Dorsal column and dorsal root ganglion degeneration causes loss of position and vibration sense, as in tabes dorsalis or Friedreich ataxia. His sensation is normal.
Central cord cavitation is a syrinx, which causes a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation.

questions.stem: His tongue atrophy and fasciculations indicate degeneration of lower motor neurons in which of the following nuclei?
options: Oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain
Facial motor nucleus in the pons
Hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla
Trigeminal motor nucleus in the pons
approach: Identify the nerve to the tongue muscles: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Place the cranial nerve nuclei by level: III and IV in the midbrain, V to VIII in the pons, IX, X, and XII in the medulla.
Tongue atrophy with fasciculations means loss of hypoglossal motor neurons in the medulla.
questions.why: The hypoglossal nucleus lies near the midline in the floor of the fourth ventricle in the medulla and supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles. Its lower motor neurons degenerate in ALS, producing tongue atrophy and fasciculations. Medullary nuclei for CN IX and X (nucleus ambiguus) are also affected, explaining his dysphagia and dysarthria (bulbar palsy). The oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nuclei are typically spared, so eye movements are preserved.
whyNot: The oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain controls most eye movements, which are spared in ALS.
The facial motor nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression, not the tongue.
Correct.
The trigeminal motor nucleus supplies the muscles of mastication, not the tongue.

topics: Cranial nerve nuclei by brainstem level

questions.stem: His right hand is atrophic with fasciculations, yet the right biceps and triceps reflexes are brisk. Which of the following best explains this combination of findings?
options: Loss of both cortical and spinal motor neurons
Compression of the C8 and T1 nerve roots in the neck
Demyelination of peripheral motor nerves and their roots
Infarction limited to the left precentral gyrus
approach: Sort the signs: atrophy and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs; brisk reflexes are an upper motor neuron sign.
Finding both in the same limb means both motor neuron levels are failing.
Mixed UMN and LMN signs with normal sensation point to ALS.
questions.why: Upper motor neuron lesions cause weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign, with little atrophy. Lower motor neuron lesions cause weakness with atrophy, fasciculations, low tone, and reduced reflexes. ALS damages both levels, so the same limb can be wasted and twitching yet hyperreflexic. Disorders limited to the anterior horn, such as poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy, cause only lower motor neuron signs.
whyNot: Correct.
Root compression causes lower motor neuron signs and reduced reflexes in that root's distribution, usually with pain or sensory loss.
Peripheral demyelination, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome, causes weakness with reduced or absent reflexes.
A cortical infarct causes upper motor neuron signs only, without atrophy or fasciculations, and would not explain the bulbar and widespread findings.

topics: Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

questions.stem: A disorder of infancy also destroys anterior horn motor neurons but spares upper motor neurons. A 3-month-old girl has generalized hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following genetic defects is most likely?
options: Dominant gain-of-function mutation in SOD1
Dystrophin gene deletion on the X chromosome
CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene
Homozygous deletion of SMN1
approach: Recognize a floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and areflexia: a pure lower motor neuron disease of infancy.
This is spinal muscular atrophy, the severe infantile form (type 1, Werdnig-Hoffmann disease).
SMA is autosomal recessive, most often from homozygous deletion of SMN1 (survival motor neuron 1).
questions.why: Spinal muscular atrophy is an autosomal recessive disease caused most often by homozygous deletion of SMN1 on chromosome 5. Without enough SMN protein, anterior horn motor neurons degenerate. The severe infantile form presents in the first months of life with profound hypotonia, areflexia, and tongue fasciculations, and death from respiratory failure is common without treatment. Upper motor neurons are spared, unlike in ALS.
whyNot: SOD1 mutations cause some familial ALS cases, which present in adults with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
Dystrophin deletions cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a muscle disease in boys that presents in early childhood with proximal weakness and calf pseudohypertrophy.
CTG expansion in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy. The congenital form causes hypotonia, but it is a muscle disease and does not cause tongue fasciculations.
Correct.
